blocks.text: Share state safely between threads by never changing it: every update produces a new object.

An **immutable object** has a state fixed at construction. With no writes to race on, it needs no locks and can be shared freely. The memory model backs this (JLS 17.5): a thread that first sees the reference after construction sees the constructor's values of its **`final` fields** and what they reach, even through a data race.

items: **Requires:** `final` fields, no setters, a `final` class or private constructor.
**Deep immutability:** fields must reference immutable objects, or be copied defensively.

blocks.text: The `final` guarantee holds only if `this` does not escape during construction, and only for state reachable through final fields.

walkthrough.note: A record's fields are `final`. The compact constructor replaces the incoming list with an unmodifiable copy, so later changes by the caller cannot leak in.
An update never mutates `this`: it builds a modified copy and returns a new `Route`. The old value stays valid for anyone still holding it.
One instance is shared by every thread through a `static final` field. Class initialization safely publishes it.
Three virtual threads derive new routes from the same base with no lock. Each `join` gives a happens-before edge, so reading `results` afterwards is safe.
The base is unchanged, and mutating the original source list after construction does not affect the copy.

blocks.text: A hot-reloadable configuration read by every request.

A service reads feature flags and rate limits on every request, and an admin endpoint reloads them from a file. Guarding a mutable map with a lock puts every request on one monitor. Instead the config is an immutable `Settings` record, and the reload builds a complete new one and swaps a single `volatile` reference. A request sees either the old or the new snapshot, never a half-updated mix.
Payoff: readers take no lock, see a consistent snapshot, and a failed parse leaves the old settings in place.

lists.title: Use when
items: State is read by many threads and rarely changes.
Values are map keys, cached, or passed between components.
You want an object that is correct without synchronization.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Large objects change often: each update copies everything.
You need in-place identity-based updates, such as counters on a hot path.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Shallow immutability: a `final` field holding an `ArrayList` is still mutable.
Letting `this` escape from the constructor voids the final-field guarantee.
Returning internal arrays or collections instead of copies or unmodifiable views.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Copying a large collection on every single-element update, when a persistent structure would do.
Immutable wrapper around a mutable service object.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records give shallow immutability for free; copy collections in the compact constructor.
`List.of`, `Map.of` and `List.copyOf` are immutable; `Collections.unmodifiableList` is only a view.

rows.difference: A builder is mutable scratch space that ends in an immutable product. It is the usual way to construct objects with many fields.
Flyweights are shared across clients, which is only safe when the shared part is immutable.
A read-write lock lets many readers share a mutable object. An immutable snapshot removes the lock, at the cost of copying on write.
A memento is an immutable snapshot of another object's state, kept so that state can be restored.

options.why: Final fields, no setters, and shift returns a new instance rather than changing this one.
Nothing clones a template to make configured variants; shift derives a value, not a copy of a prototype.
There is no step-by-step assembly or separate mutable builder.
Instances are not pooled or shared by key, though immutability would permit it.

exercises.scenario: A pricing table is read by hundreds of request threads on every call and replaced wholesale a few times a day by a reload job. Readers must never see a half-updated table.

options.why: Build a new immutable table and swap one volatile reference: no locks for readers and no torn state.
It works, but every read still takes the lock and the table must be mutated in place.
Nobody needs to wait for a condition; readers should proceed immediately.
It is for lazy one-time initialization, not for repeated replacement of shared data.

exercises.prompt: Explain why immutable objects are thread-safe, and what is needed beyond declaring fields final.

modelAnswer.text: With no writes after construction there is nothing to race on. The memory model guarantees that any thread seeing the reference sees the final fields as set by the constructor. That needs deep immutability: copy mutable inputs and never let this escape during construction.

keyPoints: No writes after construction means no races
final fields are safely visible once the constructor completes
Final reference to a mutable object is only shallow immutability
Copy defensively; do not leak this from the constructor
Updates return new instances, often swapped via a volatile reference
